---
title: "Weighty Words"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-06-18"
draft: yes
categories: [understanding]
---

When I arrived in Maryland from Korea as a child, I was placed into the fifth grade.

For the first month, I learned absolutely nothing in the classroom; I simply could not comprehend a single thing happening around me.

To survive, I carried a pocket-sized English/Korean dictionary everywhere I went.

Seeing this, my new classmates naturally wanted to help me learn.

They would crowd around, flip through my dictionary, and eagerly point out new terms for me to memorize.

Soon I realized their well-meaning curriculum consisted entirely of schoolyard slang—words that, even with my limited English, I knew better than to ever repeat at home.

It was my first introduction to the temporary, fast-fashion words of the world.

But during that pivotal May and the subsequent summer months, a much deeper education was taking place.

I wasn't just learning a language; I was filling my mind with principles that would serve me for the rest of my life.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The school I attended, Springhill Lake Elementary, had no ESL program for second-language learners because, quite simply, there were no other students like me.

Desperate to put me somewhere useful, the school partitioned off a small corner of the classroom.

Isolated behind a literal wall from my peers, I was given a mechanical device to run cards through—early audio tools with a magnetic strip that uttered key vocabulary terms in a sterile, monotone.

This mechanical isolation was a minor improvement over schoolyard slang, but the true trajectory of my life was being shaped elsewhere, beyond those temporary school provided walls.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The antidote to my isolation arrived in the form of a volunteer: Mrs. Johnson, the wife of our local congregation's Bishop.

She didn't use mechanical tools or linguistic shortcuts. Instead, she sat with me and read books—mainly reading *to* me.

Her voice and undivided attention provided a refreshing sanctuary from children's television programs and mechanical devices that were substitues and used to fill my days at school.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

At home, my parents provided the final, crucial layers to this curriculum.

When we immigrated, we were limited to things that can be packed into checked luggages.

Packed alongside my pocket dictionary was a six-volume set of books that summarized the Old and New Testaments, complete with historical and archaeological photographs.

For a child who couldn't yet read the books in the school library, these volumes became my main source of both information and entertainment.

I devoured them and memorizing key events and its heroes.

Looking back, my true curriculum during those first few months in America was forged by a very specific coalition: the patient reading sessions with Mrs. Johnson, the extended support of a church community, the dedication of my parents and sisters, and the ancient stories inside those volume of books in Korean.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

By modern standards, these resources were scarce and hardly adequate.

Yet, their very scarcity forced a structural focus.

Because I was denied the noisy, passing memes and cultural trends of the day, I was fed a steady diet of the timeless.

They established an intellectual and spiritual bedrock that I have visited over and over again throughout my life.

It taught me early that the strength of a life is not built on the shifting sands of what is momentarily popular, but on the quiet, deliberate practice of absorbing things that endure—like reading together from books that have not only withstood the passage of time, but have also allowed people to endure and overcome.
